hooks.text: Air pressure sealed three astronauts inside a burning cabin.
Why couldn't three astronauts open a door during a fire?
NASA thought their most dangerous test was perfectly safe.

title: The Fire That Reshaped NASA
description: Apollo 1 was supposed to be a safe ground test until a design flaw trapped the crew inside a burning cabin.

beats.text: Air pressure sealed three astronauts inside a burning cabin.
beats.visual: official portrait of Apollo 1 crew Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee, 1967

beats.text: Most people think the Apollo 1 crew died in space.
beats.visual: artist concept of an Apollo command module orbiting the Earth

beats.text: But the disaster happened during a routine test on the ground.
beats.visual: photograph of the Apollo 1 Saturn IB rocket on Launch Complex 34, 1967
subjects: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station Launch Complex 34

beats.text: NASA considered it safe because the rocket was unfueled.
beats.visual: detailed close-up of the Saturn IB rocket stages

beats.text: Inside, the cabin held pure oxygen at extremely high pressure.
beats.visual: photograph of the interior controls and seats of an Apollo command module

beats.text: A single electrical arc turned the cockpit into a furnace.
beats.visual: photograph of the fire-damaged interior of the Apollo 1 command module, 1967

beats.text: Rising pressure forced the inward-opening hatch shut like a cork.
beats.visual: technical diagram of the Apollo Block I inward-opening plug door hatch

beats.text: This failure forced NASA to invent the outward-swinging emergency hatch.
beats.visual: photograph of the redesigned Apollo Block II outward-opening hatch

beats.text: Before that fix, air pressure sealed three astronauts inside.
beats.visual: photograph of the memorial plaque at the abandoned Launch Complex 34
subjects: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station Launch Complex 34

better_than_last: Applied the myth_vs_fact structure to contrast the perceived safety of a ground test with the mechanical reality of the hatch trap.
